title: New Tariffs Raise the Risk of a More Hawkish Fed, Economists Warn
excerpt: Proposed duties on 14 trading partners would lift the effective US tariff rate above 13%, economists estimate, just as core PCE inflation printed 3.3% in October.
body:
• Economists say the Trump administration's newly proposed tariffs raise the risk of a more hawkish Federal Reserve — rate hikes, and rates held higher for longer.
  • The proposals follow an eight-month excess-capacity investigation covering 14 trading partners; economists estimate they would lift the US effective tariff rate from 11.2% to above 13% if implemented.
  • Core PCE inflation rose 3.3% year on year in October, above the 3.2% expected; the Fed is widely expected to raise rates by a quarter point next month.
  • For borrowers: markets already expect at least one more hike in the first quarter, keeping mortgage, card and loan costs elevated into 2027.

A fresh round of proposed US tariffs raises the likelihood that the Federal Reserve will have to raise interest rates and keep them higher for longer to combat the inflationary pressure the duties create, economists told Yahoo Finance. The administration proposed the tariffs on Wednesday, following an eight-month investigation into excess manufacturing capacity in 14 major trading partners.

"The concern is that tariffs add another supply-side cost shock at a time when demand remains resilient enough for businesses to pass a larger share of those costs through to consumers."

— Greg Daco, chief economist at EY

Why tariffs complicate the Fed's job

Greg Daco, chief economist at EY, said the new tariffs raise the risk of "a more hawkish Fed response" given that inflation is at a three-year high. He expects more policymakers may favour raising rates earlier as evidence of inflation persistence builds, rather than waiting until pressures become embedded and potentially require more hikes later.

Many Fed members, including New York Fed President John Williams, had been sanguine that tariffs were largely washing out of the inflation picture. Williams warned this week that could change: "The encouraging news is that the effects of tariffs on inflation have largely abated and should not add significantly to inflation in goods prices in the future. Of course, this could change if new tariffs were introduced."

The inflation backdrop

The Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge showed prices heating up more than expected in October: the "core" Personal Consumption Expenditures index rose 3.3 percent year on year, against expectations of 3.2 percent and up from 3.1 percent in September, with core prices steady at 0.3 percent month on month. TheStreet reported that revised third-quarter GDP growth of 4.3 percent — the fastest pace since late 2023 — gives central bankers further reason to lean hawkish, and that futures traders see roughly a 97 to 98 percent probability of a 25-basis-point hike at the December 8-9 FOMC meeting, according to the CME Group FedWatch Tool.

Replacement, not pure escalation — mostly

Economists largely view the proposed tariffs not as an escalation but as a replacement for the 2025 levies struck down by the Supreme Court. They would bring the US effective tariff rate from 11.2 percent back up to above 13 percent, on par with the previous emergency-powers level. Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM, warned the proposal could produce higher-than-expected goods prices in the first quarter, when companies typically reset prices: "If implemented as proposed, it will result in a large drag on U.S. goods imports through the end of the decade, which will be accompanied by rising inflation via the goods channel."

Not everyone is alarmed. Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics, said the announcement "is not as alarming as it looks," because the new tariffs essentially replace previously announced Section 301 tariffs related to forced-labor concerns — though they would still provide a marginal boost to prices and keep core goods inflation firm into next year, and the option of raising tariffs further if trade talks fail is an upside risk to inflation.

What to watch

The Fed is widely expected to raise rates next month by a quarter percentage point, with markets already expecting at least one more hike in the first quarter. For households, the practical read-through is borrowing costs staying elevated for longer: each additional hike feeds into credit-card, auto and adjustable-rate borrowing, and analysts cited by TheStreet warn sustained tightening could keep Treasury yields — and with them mortgage rates — high well into 2027.
